content: Two experts, one specializing in the GRADE methodology and the other in clinical expertise related to sexually transmitted infections (STIs), reviewed the recommendations. After discussions, it was determined that additional information was necessary. Consequently, the recommendations for syphilis screening were developed during subsequent teleconferences and electronic communications with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) working group for syphilis. To formulate these recommendations, the GDG working group carefully evaluated the benefits and risks of the interventions, the importance of the outcomes, associated costs and resource use, acceptability to stakeholders (including individuals affected by STIs), impact on health equity, and feasibility of implementation. Judgments were made for each of these criteria, and the overall strength of each recommendation was determined. In cases of disagreement, the GDG planned to vote and record the results; however, consensus was reached during discussions, and no votes were necessary. The finalized recommendations were approved electronically by all GDG members after teleconference discussions. The guideline was then written in full and underwent peer review. An External Review Group approved the methods and agreed with the recommendations, as detailed in Annex A. Using the GRADE approach, the strength of each recommendation was classified as either strong or conditional. Strong recommendations were phrased as The WHO STI guideline recommends…, while conditional recommendations were phrased as The WHO STI guideline suggests…. The implications of these recommendations for patients, clinicians, and policymakers were explained in detail. Conflict of interest management was a priority throughout the guideline development process. WHO's Declaration of Interest (DOI) procedures were followed, and DOI statements were obtained from all GDG members before their participation. At GDG meetings in December 2013 and October 2015, members disclosed any interests at the start of the meetings. Any disclosed interests were minor, unrelated to STIs, or involved non-commercial grants. The STI team determined that no significant conflicts of interest existed that would exclude any member from full participation in the guideline development process. The guideline will be disseminated as a printed publication, a downloadable document on the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research website, and through the WHO Reproductive Health Library. It will also be available in a guideline application created using GRADEpro GDT software. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices to support countries in adapting, implementing, and monitoring the guideline. External partners, including UNFPA, UNICEF, UNAIDS, NGOs, and other agencies, will assist in disseminating and implementing the recommendations. The guideline will also be presented at major conferences related to STIs and HIV. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating the recommendations will be established within a year of implementation. An electronic follow-up survey of key end-users will be conducted after publication to identify challenges, evaluate the guideline's usefulness, and address gaps in future editions. The recommendations for syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women emphasize universal screening during the first antenatal care visit, regardless of syphilis prevalence in the setting. This strong recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence showing significant benefits, including reductions in stillbirths, neonatal deaths, and congenital syphilis cases. Universal screening is also cost-effective, equitable, and acceptable to both patients and healthcare providers. In settings with low screening coverage, high loss to follow-up, or limited laboratory capacity, the guideline suggests using on-site rapid syphilis tests (RSTs) rather than standard off-site laboratory-based screening. In low-prevalence settings, a single on-site RST is preferred over a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test. In high-prevalence settings, a sequence of tests, including an RST followed by RPR testing and treatment based on syphilis duration, is suggested. These conditional recommendations are based on low-quality evidence. The guideline also addresses treatment strategies for pregnant women who test positive for syphilis. Benzathine penicillin remains the recommended treatment, as it effectively treats both the mother and fetus. Alternative treatments, such as erythromycin or azithromycin, are suggested with caution in cases of penicillin unavailability, as these do not adequately treat the fetus. Stock-outs of benzathine penicillin should be avoided due to the severe risks of untreated syphilis during pregnancy. Countries are encouraged to adapt the guidelines based on local epidemiology and resources. If existing antenatal syphilis screening systems are inadequate, new strategies, including the use of RSTs, should be considered. Accurate baseline data on syphilis prevalence and the quality of testing and treatment systems are essential for effective implementation.
